name: Replace main turbine components
summary: When a gearbox, generator, main bearing or blade fails, the turbine stays down until the component is swapped with a large crane. The site manager confirms the failure, chooses a new or refurbished part, gets the spend approved and has a buyer order the component and book a crawler crane and contractors. Lead times of weeks to months for the part, crane availability, preparing a crane pad on farmland and waiting for a few calm days for the lift keep a turbine down for weeks, while the crane costs about a thousand dollars an hour whether it is lifting or standing by.

baseline.org_archetype: An Alberta-centred listed generator with about 450 mostly older wind turbines in southern Alberta that rents large crawler cranes from crane contractors for main component exchanges.
baseline.notes: Wind division of about 70 people running roughly 450 turbines on 11 to 12 southern Alberta wind farms commissioned between 1997 and 2021, most of them older 0.66 to 3 MW machines without tower elevators.

trigger: A main component work request arrives from technicians who found a failed gearbox, generator, main bearing or blade, or from inspection and condition monitoring findings.
end_state: The new component is installed and commissioned, the turbine is back in service, the crane has left, the failed component is shipped for repair or warranty, and the work order is closed with costs and failure data.

volume.seasonality: Lifts cluster from late spring to autumn when calm days are more frequent and ground conditions allow crane access; winter failures often wait for spring. Road bans during spring thaw delay crane moves.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate (about 24 a year, or 5 percent of about 450 turbines a year). Main component failures are an expected part of wind O&M (res2023); the rate is not sourced.

systems.name: ERP (finance, purchasing and plant maintenance modules)
Hydro, wind and battery SCADA and remote control
Document management and engineering drawings repository

Two-person wind technician team with service truck

steps.name: Review the findings and confirm the work request
steps.description: The site manager reads the work request, photos, oil and vibration data, opens the turbine's history in the ERP and historian, and decides whether the evidence already shows a main component failure or needs an inspection first.

next.condition: failure obvious: seized gearbox, broken blade, burnt generator

evidence.note: Detection through monitoring, inspection and engineer observation (source); timing estimated.

steps.name: Inspect the component to confirm the failure
steps.description: A technician pair climbs the turbine with a borescope, vibration meter and oil sample kit, inspects gear teeth, bearings or the blade, and reports the damage and whether an up-tower repair is possible.

error.defect_description: Damage underestimated, so the wrong scope is ordered.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Parts 2, 9 and 15: hazard assessment, fall protection and lockout for every climb

evidence.note: Ultrasound and borescope inspection used to confirm main component damage (source); timing estimated.

steps.name: Decide the exchange approach
steps.description: The site manager decides between a new component, a refurbished unit from a repairer or the fleet pool, and the manufacturer or an independent service company, weighing price, lead time, warranty and the turbine's remaining life.

error.defect_description: Cheaper refurbished unit chosen with a lead time longer than expected.

evidence.note: Lead times of three to six months for some components drive the choice (source); options described from common practice.

steps.name: Prepare the cost estimate and approval request
steps.description: The site manager builds a cost estimate in a spreadsheet (component, crane, crane pad, contractors, own labour, lost energy) and writes a short approval request with the exchange plan.

error.defect_description: Crane standby or crane pad cost left out of the estimate.

evidence.note: Crane costs of 50,000 to 150,000 USD per gearbox exchange (source) are a large share of the estimate; preparation time estimated.

steps.name: Approve the spend
steps.description: The director of wind and storage reviews the estimate against the maintenance budget and approves it, asks for more information, or sends it up when it exceeds the director's limit.

control.basis: Company delegation of financial authority for maintenance spend

evidence.note: Exchanges cost several hundred thousand dollars, above a site manager's limit; approval wait estimated.

steps.name: Check fleet spares
steps.description: The site manager checks the ERP and the spares list for a matching gearbox, generator, bearing or blade held in company stock or in a pool agreement, and reserves it if there is one.

evidence.note: Share of exchanges served from spares or a pool is the author's estimate for a fleet with many identical older turbines.

steps.name: Source the component and issue the purchase order
steps.description: The buyer gets quotes from the manufacturer and refurbishers, checks delivery dates and warranty terms, writes a sole-source justification when only the manufacturer can supply, and issues the purchase order in the ERP.

control.basis: Procurement policy: competitive quotes above a threshold or a documented sole-source justification

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the component
steps.description: The turbine stays down while the supplier builds, refurbishes or ships the component; gearboxes and blades for older models can take months, and refurbished units depend on the repairer's queue.

error.defect_description: Component arrives with the wrong interface or damaged in transport.

evidence.note: Lead times for some components average three to six months, with nine months for one main shaft (source); the low and mode (two and five weeks) reflect pool and refurbished units that arrive sooner, the high is six months.

steps.name: Book the crane and contractors
steps.description: The buyer asks crane contractors for availability and rates, books a crawler crane and crew to arrive when the component is due, and issues service orders to the crane company and the lifting and civil contractors; for parts on order this booking is made during the wait for the component.

error.defect_description: Crane booked for a date that does not match the component delivery.

control.basis: Contractor prequalification: only contractors with a current safety certification and approved insurance

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for a crane slot
steps.description: The site waits for the booked crane, which may be finishing a job at another wind farm or construction site; in the busy construction season large cranes are booked weeks ahead.

evidence.note: Residual wait after booking during the component lead time; estimate.

steps.name: Prepare the crane pad and access
steps.description: A civil contractor builds or repairs the crane pad and widens the access road at the turbine after the landowner has been notified; spring road bans and soft ground can delay the work.

evidence.note: Conventional cranes usually need a crane pad (source); timing and road-ban effects estimated. Contractor working time is folded into the wait.

steps.name: Review the lift plan and permits
steps.description: The site manager reviews the crane contractor's critical lift plan, the manufacturer's exchange procedure and the site safety plan, checks wind limits for the lift and signs the permits.

error.defect_description: Lift plan wind limit or ground bearing check not verified.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 6 (cranes, hoists and lifting devices): lift plan for critical lifts and operation within the manufacturer's load and wind limits

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Mobilise and assemble the crane
steps.description: The crane arrives on many trucks, and the crane crew assembles the boom and counterweights on the pad over one to several days, then completes its pre-lift inspection.

evidence.note: A conventional crane must be procured and assembled before the lift (source); durations estimated. Crane hours are charged rental hours of about 10 per day.

steps.name: Wait for a calm weather window
steps.description: The crane stands by on site until the forecast shows the few calm days the lift needs; the decision to lift is made a day or two ahead and the crane is paid for while it waits.

evidence.note: A three-to-four-day weather window is needed and is hard to find at windy sites; mobilisation decided 24 to 72 hours ahead (source). Standby hours estimated.

steps.name: Prepare the turbine for the lift
steps.description: The technicians lock out the turbine and rotor, drain oil, disconnect cables, couplings and cooling lines, remove the nacelle roof sections and rig the component with the crane crew.

error.defect_description: Connection missed during disconnection, delaying the lift.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 (energy isolation) and Part 9 (fall protection); company permit-to-work standard

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Lift out the failed component and install the new one
steps.description: With the crane, the crew lowers the failed component (sometimes the whole rotor first), lifts the replacement into place and bolts it down, stopping whenever gusts exceed the lift limit.

error.defect_description: Misalignment or bolting error on installation.

control.basis: Crane manufacturer wind limits and the approved critical lift plan

evidence.note: Removing a gearbox takes about three days once the crane is assembled, sometimes with the rotor lowered (source).

steps.name: Reconnect, align, fill and torque
steps.description: The technicians reconnect couplings, cables and cooling lines, align the drivetrain with laser tools, fill oil, torque all bolts to the manufacturer's values and refit the nacelle covers.

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Commission and test run
steps.description: With the manufacturer's representative the technicians run the turbine through commissioning tests, check vibration, temperatures and noise, and sign the commissioning record.

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Demobilise the crane
steps.description: The crane crew dismantles the boom and counterweights and trucks the crane off site, and the civil contractor restores the access road and pad area.

evidence.note: Crane removal is a separate stage after the exchange (source); hours estimated.

steps.name: Return the turbine to service
steps.description: The operations centre operator takes the turbine back into remote control, restarts it, checks power against the power curve and marks it available, ending the long outage in the availability record.

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Ship the failed component for repair or warranty
steps.description: The site manager arranges transport of the failed component to the manufacturer or a repairer, files a warranty claim if it applies, and issues a repair service order so the unit can return to the spares pool.

error.defect_description: Warranty claim missed or filed late.

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Close the work order with costs and failure data
steps.description: The site manager records the failure mode, root cause, component serial numbers, hours and costs on the ERP work order and closes it, so reliability engineers can track main component failures across the fleet.

error.defect_description: Root cause or serial numbers not recorded.

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve crane and contractor tickets
steps.description: The site manager checks the crane and contractor field tickets against the booked hours, standby days and service orders, disputes errors and approves them in the ERP for invoice matching.

control.basis: Delegation of authority and three-way match of service orders, field tickets and invoices

evidence.note: Common practice for onshore wind main component exchanges in 2019-2022; author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Long component lead time
exceptions.description: No spare is available and the manufacturer or repairer quotes three months or more, so the turbine is down for a season.

exceptions.name: Crane standing by for wind
exceptions.description: The crane is assembled but gusts stay above the lift limit for several days; standby hours are charged.

exceptions.name: Commissioning problem
exceptions.description: Vibration, a leak or misalignment shows up in the test run and the drivetrain is reworked.

benchmarks.unit: USD per gearbox exchange, crane only

evidence.note: Stated in the source; depends on wind farm location. The simulated crane cost here (about 1,300 CAD/h for about 70 to 80 charged hours) falls in this range.

benchmarks.unit: months, average for some main components

evidence.note: Stated in the source; one main shaft took nine months.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from work request to tickets approved
benchmarks.population: Author's estimate for an Alberta fleet of older turbines

evidence.note: Combines component lead times of weeks (spares, pool units) to three to six months (res2023), approvals, crane booking and weather windows; not measured. The organisation file describes the turbine as down for weeks; the cited lead times point to months for about two thirds of cases.

pain_points.description: Component lead times of months keep a turbine down for a season unless a spare is on hand.

evidence.note: Three to six month lead times (source).

pain_points.description: The crane is paid by the hour while it waits for a calm window, so a windy week can add tens of thousands of dollars.

evidence.note: Weather windows hard to find at windy sites (res2023); crane costs of 50,000 to 150,000 USD per exchange (wpe2015).

pain_points.description: Approval, sourcing and crane booking run one after another through people with other priorities, adding weeks before the lift.

evidence.note: Author's judgement.

sources.title: How can we prepare for main component failure? (B. McDaid)
sources.supports: Main component failures (gearboxes, bearings, generators, main shafts, blades) are an expected part of O&M; lead times for some components average three to six months (nine months for one main shaft); a crane exchange needs a three-to-four-day weather window that is hard to find at windy sites; crane mobilisation decisions are made 24 to 72 hours ahead; condition monitoring, oil readings and inspection give early warning.

sources.title: Clever crane lowers the cost of gearbox swaps (P. Dvorak)
sources.supports: Conventional crane costs of 50,000 to 150,000 USD per gearbox exchange depending on site location; a conventional crane must be procured and assembled and usually needs a crane pad; removing a gearbox takes about three days once the crane is assembled, sometimes with the rotor lowered to the ground.

assumptions: Triggers: 80 percent from technicians' repair visits (the organisation file's only link), 10 percent from defects found during scheduled service and 10 percent from condition monitoring and oil analysis by the reliability group. The last two links are not in the organisation file.

Crane hours are charged rental hours (about 10 a day) for assembly, standby, lifting and removal; the contractor's working time on the pad, mobilisation and demobilisation is folded into waits because it is not this organisation's labour.

touch_min records the lead technician's minutes; a crew of about four technicians works the lift days, so the wind_technician FTE (2.2) is the lead's roughly 40 hands-on hours per exchange times about four people at two exchanges a month, less the inspection climb done by a pair.
Up-tower repairs that avoid a crane are not modelled separately; they are a minority of main component cases for this fleet.
The process map volume (1 to 5 a month) is kept; it implies about 5 percent of turbines a year, which is the author's estimate for an older fleet and not sourced.
roc_operator is added for the return to service; the organisation file does not list this role for the process.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (wage x 1.40). Crane cost per hour is the organisation file's resource estimate.

Organisation file corrected on 2026-11-24: the lift-day steps now carry people 4 and the inspection and commissioning steps people 2, so the staffing check counts the crew rather than the lead technician only.
